explanation: A resource-dependency edge means an owner can hold one lock before requesting the next. A directed cycle permits circular waiting, so admit only an acyclic combined dependency graph. Build each candidate graph from the complete active per-owner orders before committing: deleting candidate edges on rejection can accidentally remove an edge still needed by another owner. Keep per-owner request positions separately so an invalid lookup never silently skips a required acquisition. Python creates independent reachability rows and copies accepted paths. Candidate rebuild selects the new path without modifying active orders, so rejection requires no destructive rollback. None is distinct from a granted ResourceLock object, and each constructed factory owns separate order/cursor lists.
correctness: Initially every owner order is empty and the graph has no edges. For Declare, validate bounds/distinctness before indexing. Rebuild the candidate union using the new path only for the target owner, and compute reachability by Floyd-Warshall. After processing intermediate vertices through k, reach[i][j] exactly describes paths whose internal vertices are among those processed; induction over k establishes complete reachability. A true diagonal entry is exactly a directed cycle, so rejection and admission follow the stated graph policy. No live state changes until admission; cloning the order and resetting only its cursor preserves other owners and caller independence. GetLock compares only the next pending resource and advances exactly on a match, returning the stable provided identity. Thus clients following granted orders obey the admitted resource DAG. A circular wait would imply a resource-dependency cycle, impossible in that DAG; finite clients under eventual scheduling complete and release their locks.
walkthrough: With 3 resources, owner 0 declares [0,1] (accept), owner 1 declares [1,2] (accept), and owner 2 declares [2,0] (reject: 0→1→2→0 would be cyclic). GetLock(0,1) returns null and leaves 0 pending. GetLock(0,0) then GetLock(0,1) return the actual locks 0 and 1. Owner 1 can obtain 1 then 2; owner 2 has no accepted order. After owner 0 is exhausted, another GetLock(0,1) returns null. The native clients may contend on lock 1, but no circular wait exists.
timeComplexity: Declare takes O(R^3 + sum(active order lengths) + new order length), dominated by O(R^3) for R resources and four owners with distinct-resource paths. GetLock takes O(1) bookkeeping plus the provided constant-time pool lookup. Native client acquisition waiting is outside these administration-method costs.
spaceComplexity: O(sum(active order lengths)+4) persistent factory state and O(R^2) temporary reachability/seen storage per Declare, excluding the borrowed native lock pool and client threads. Returned locks are borrowed identities, not copies or owned allocations.
edgeCases: Empty order, invalid signed indices, repeated resources and exhausted lookups.
Atomic rejection, shared edges belonging to several owners and replacement that removes only one owner old dependencies.
Out-of-order GetLock must not consume the next resource.
Caller changes its old array; independent factory instances share a pool without sharing orders.
Acyclic nonnumeric resource orders are valid; no global ascending-order restriction is imposed.
